events.description: Signed up for the evening vocational instructor course after twenty-four years on the machines.
Merged shift handover notes into the fault log notebook, ending the morning disputes about the night shift.
Tried the earlier bus to gain sleep before nights, with no change in how he arrived.
First written assignment returned with comments; noticed hand-taught material sticks and read material does not.
Began sending Kamil workshop photographs with a question about one part instead of asking about his job.
Management announced a review of the number two line, the oldest in the country.
Two hospital visits to Zenon, who refused to talk about the mill either time.
Set the goal of finishing his working life in the training bay rather than on the machines.
Moved heavy allotment work to the morning after nights instead of lying down immediately; sleep lengthened.
Put his name down for the training-bay post in March; no news followed.
Offered to cover half of Kamil's deposit; the offer went unanswered.
Listened to recorded lectures while filing at the bench and passed the theory paper.
Zenon died in December; the funeral filled the chapel with three generations of fitters.
Slawek brought the mill's old fire-station motorcycle into the garage as a joint project.
Bogdan denied the training-bay role had been promised, contradicting Iwona's shortlist email.
Separated turnaround ache from the flat grey that follows a week of nights.
Had Piotr explain the pump back to him, exposing three steps he had skipped in his own demonstration.
Kamil's Norwegian contract confirmed as a six-weeks-there, two-weeks-home rotation.
Union representative confirmed the posting decision had gone nowhere for four months.
Sorted Zenon's inherited toolbox onto the bench in his old size order, one Saturday in February.
Filmed his assessed demonstration a week early and watched it silently, spotting that he blocked the workpiece.
Cut coffee after eight in the evening with no discernible effect.
Marek reported being told a different timeline for the same post.
Asked Kamil what he would need in his first month abroad instead of arguing about the move.
Agreed with Slawek to work on the bike only when both are present, ending the stalled parts pile.
Submitted logbook hours to the course coordinator; confirmation never arrived.
Post frozen, but two shifts a week reassigned to the training bay from April.
Piotr assigned to him formally as first apprentice under the new arrangement.
Kamil spent two evenings of his home rotation in the garage with the bike.
Kamil telephoned from Norway unprompted for the first time.

dialogue.text: I'm Tomasz, fifty-two, and I have been a maintenance fitter at the paper mill here for twenty-four years. In September I signed up for the evening instructor course, which at my age feels slightly ridiculous.
Twenty-four years of doing the work and now a classroom about how to teach it. Where does the ridiculous part come from?
I did my technikum in 1991 and have not sat behind a desk since. Half the people on the course could be my children, and they type notes while I am still finding the page.
Thirty years is a long time to be away from that particular kind of room. Speed of typing is not the same thing as knowing the machine.

sessions.summary: Tomasz, fifty-two, a paper mill fitter of twenty-four years, starts an evening instructor course three decades after his last classroom and feels out of place.

dialogue.text: I'm the oldest man on the maintenance crew now, and every morning handover had turned into an argument about what did or did not happen on nights.
Everyone defending their own eight hours before the first coffee. That sours a whole shift before it starts.
So I started keeping the handover notes in the same notebook as the fault log instead of on loose paper, and the morning arguments stopped inside three weeks.
One book, one version of the night. Nobody has to remember who said what when it's written next to the fault.

dialogue.text: I'm Polish, born in Bydgoszcz and still living twenty minutes from the house I grew up in. Thirty years of rotating shifts and my body has started sending me the bill.
Three decades of asking your body to sleep on someone else's timetable. It tends to submit that invoice around now.
I tried swapping to the earlier bus so I could get a couple of hours before the night shift, and I still arrive flat.
So the extra time was available and the sleep wasn't. Those are two different problems wearing the same clothes.

sessions.summary: Thirty years of rotating shifts are catching up with Tomasz in his home city, and an earlier bus taken to gain sleep leaves him arriving just as flat.

The trouble is the whole assessment is written. Nobody is going to grade me on rebuilding a gearbox.
So the thing you're best at is the thing that earns no marks. That gap is going to need managing, not fixing.

dialogue.text: My son Kamil is twenty-four and answers my calls with three words. Halina says I only ever ring him to check up on him, and she is not entirely wrong.
Three words is a door held mostly closed. And your wife has named what he is probably hearing on the other end of it.
So instead of asking him how the job is going, I started sending him photographs of whatever is on my workbench with a question about one part, and he answers within the hour now.
You gave him something to answer instead of something to account for. The bench turned out to be easier ground than his week.

dialogue.text: Management have announced a review of the number two line. Everyone knows what a review means, and nobody will say the word.
A word everyone is carrying and nobody is putting down. That silence does its own damage across a shift.
That line has run three shifts a day since 1974 and it is the oldest machine of its kind still working in the country.
Fifty years of continuous running, and now under review. The machine has outlasted most of the people who were told it would.
One thing, if you don't mind. Say back what you have understood before you ask me anything. I find questions easier to answer once I know you have followed.
Then what I have understood is this: the line is under review, everyone knows what that means, and the not-saying is heavier than the saying would be. Questions can wait.

sessions.summary: A review of the fifty-year-old number two line goes unspoken across the shifts, and Tomasz asks to hear understanding reflected back before any questions.

dialogue.text: Zenon, the foreman who trained me in ninety-nine, is in the hospital on Ujejskiego. I went twice and neither time did he want to talk about the mill at all.
What I understand: you went with the mill in your pocket, and he had already put it down. Two visits and the one subject you share was closed.
He wanted to talk about his brother's boat. I know nothing about boats. I sat there for an hour and understood one sentence in three.
An hour of not understanding, given anyway. That is a different sort of visit than the one you planned, and probably the one he wanted.

dialogue.text: Let me say the point of all this out loud for once: I want to finish out my working life in the training bay instead of on the machines, and the certificate is the only door into that room.
What I hear is a specific ending you're aiming at, not just an escape from shifts. The certificate is the key, not the goal.
Thirteen years left if I go at sixty-five. I would rather spend them showing twenty-year-olds how not to lose a finger than climbing over a hot machine at four in the morning.
Thirteen years is long enough to matter and short enough to plan. And you have already named exactly what you want to be doing in them.

dialogue.text: Something worked, finally. I stopped going straight to bed after nights and did the heavy digging at the allotment first, and I now sleep four solid hours instead of two broken ones.
What I understand: lying down was the plan and staying asleep was the problem. Two hours of spade first, and the body arrived at bed already finished.
Halina thinks I have lost my mind, digging potatoes at eight in the morning after twelve hours on the machines.
It does look mad from the kitchen window. It also works, which is the only test that matters here.

A chapel full of people who all learned the same hands. That is the size of what has gone.
He trained more than half the fitters who have ever worked in that plant. There is nobody left who was there before him.
So the line back through the plant ends with him. You are all standing at the front of it now, whether or not anyone said so.
For a while, do not offer me anything to do about any of this. I do not want steps. I want to say it and have it heard, and that is all.
Then I will hold it and not hand anything back. Say as much or as little as you want.

His initials are punched into the handles. I am not going to file them off.

dialogue.text: The training-bay question is answered at last, and not the way anyone expected. The post itself stays frozen, but from April I am in the bay two shifts a week and on the machines the other three.
Not the title, but the room. After fourteen months of nobody's desk, someone finally moved something.
Piotr is assigned to me as the first one. Jacek says once the roster shows it for a year, the post has to follow the practice.
So the roster becomes the argument. Doing the job visibly for a year is a stronger case than any shortlist email.

sessions.summary: The frozen post is bypassed: from April Tomasz spends two shifts a week in the training bay with Piotr assigned to him, three shifts still on the machines.

dialogue.text: Kamil was home for his two weeks. Both evenings that I expected the usual silence at the kitchen table, the two of us were out in the garage with the bike until midnight instead. He rang me from Norway on the Tuesday, which in twenty-four years he has never once done.
The kitchen table always wanted a conversation. The garage only wanted two people facing the same engine, and that turned out to be the easier place to talk.
He asked whether the bike would be finished by his next rotation. I said only if he is standing there, because Slawek and I have a rule.
You just extended the rule to include him. That is an invitation with a date on it, which is harder to let slide than a phone call.

sessions.summary: Kamil spends both home evenings in the garage rather than at the kitchen table, then telephones from Norway unprompted for the first time in twenty-four years.
